claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Mg is uniformly distributed in the initial alloy.
Thermal exposure at approximately 500–700°C activates Mg diffusion out of the metastable matrix.
Mg diffusion produces localized clustering and nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially form and grow at grain boundaries.
Aged samples will have a larger volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates than the initial state.
Aged samples will have coarser Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates than the initial state.
Intermetallic phase separation creates surface compositional heterogeneity.
Surface compositional heterogeneity compromises the continuity of the protective oxide layer.
Loss of oxide-layer continuity causes corrosion resistance to decline.
Loss of oxide-layer continuity causes high-temperature oxidation resistance to decline.
Corrosion degradation after aging will be detectable as increased passivation current or lower electrochemical impedance.
The initial homogeneous metastable alloy has robust corrosion resistance.
The initial homogeneous metastable alloy has robust oxidation resistance.
Significant microstructural evolution is expected during oxidizing exposure at approximately 500–700°C.
At lower temperatures, Mg diffusion and intermetallic-nucleation kinetics are too slow to cause significant microstructural evolution.
In inert atmospheres, Mg diffusion and intermetallic-nucleation kinetics are too limited to cause significant microstructural evolution.
